description: R.E.M.'s jangly Velvet Underground cover — cut as a 1983 B-side and later collected on the rarities album Dead Letter Office — heard here in the official UMG audio upload.

pops.text: Lou Reed wrote this one — it first appeared on The Velvet Underground & Nico, the famous 'banana album,' in 1967.
R.E.M. recorded it as the B-side of the 1983 I.R.S. re-recording of 'Radio Free Europe,' the single that broke them nationally.
It was an early tell of the band's roots: from the very start, the Athens upstarts weren't shy about exposing their Velvet Underground influence.
The take is loose and live-in-the-studio — R.E.M. sounding like a bar band running a favorite song, not polishing a hit.
The track resurfaced in 1987 on Dead Letter Office, R.E.M.'s odds-and-sods compilation of B-sides and outtakes.
Dead Letter Office actually holds three Velvet Underground covers: this one, plus 'Pale Blue Eyes' and 'Femme Fatale.'
Guitarist Peter Buck was a famous Velvet Underground devotee, and the band kept covering their songs throughout its career.
R.E.M.'s version later turned up as a bonus track on deluxe reissues of their debut album Murmur.
In February 2025, Buck and Mike Mills played this song in Athens with Michael Shannon's R.E.M. tribute band — and Patti Smith guitarist Lenny Kaye sitting in.
Check the credits on this official upload: songwriter is simply 'Lou Reed.' One legend covering another.

title: There She Goes Again

description: The Stones' icy-hot rocker from Emotional Rescue, in its official 1980 promo video directed by David Mallet — Mick strutting, the band freezing him out.

pops.text: Written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards for Emotional Rescue (1980), the Stones' follow-up to Some Girls.
It was recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York in late 1979 and January 1980.
The whole hook is a flipped cliché: 'I'm so hot for her — and she's so cold.'
That's longtime Stones sideman Bobby Keys honking on saxophone.
The percussion comes from Michael Shrieve — yes, Santana's Woodstock drummer — sitting in with the Stones.
Released as a single in the US, it peaked at #26 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Emotional Rescue itself topped the album charts in both the US and the UK.
This promo was directed by David Mallet, one of the busiest music-video directors of the early MTV era.
Despite the single's success, the song became a live rarity — by 2024 the Stones had played it only nine times in 17 years.
It finally returned to the setlist on the Hackney Diamonds tour in Glendale, Arizona, in May 2024 — its first performance in five years.

title: She's So Cold

description: A two-minute electronic miniature from promptgenix's album Digital Delta: volume four, self-released through DistroKid in February 2026 — heard in its official auto-generated YouTube upload.

pops.text: This track was released on February 9, 2026, as part of the album Digital Delta: volume four.
It was distributed through DistroKid under the imprint name 10302836 Records DK.
Songwriting and composing credits go to 'C T C,' per the track's official metadata.
Production is credited to promptgenix — a fully independent, do-it-yourself digital release.
Blink and it's over: the whole track runs just 2 minutes and 20 seconds.
As the title hints, Digital Delta: volume four is the fourth volume in promptgenix's Digital Delta series.
The album's song titles read like dispatches from a weird news day: 'We Kept Posting Through It,' 'Emergency Tone (Stuck On Loop),' 'Fire Drills Became the World.'
Shazam's listening data says fans most often identify this song at around the 35-second mark.
There's no staged music video — this auto-generated YouTube upload, delivered by DistroKid, is the song's official video presence.
The track has already had a second life as soundtrack music in fan-made gaming montage videos on YouTube.

title: They'll Call This an Accident

description: An official-channel live performance from the Classic Center in Athens, Georgia, on February 10, 2011 — night one of Widespread Panic's 25th anniversary run, with 'Pigeons' opening the second set.

pops.text: This is one of Panic's oldest songs — an early version surfaced at a house party in Athens on October 23, 1986, the year the band formed.
Before it was 'Pigeons,' the song carried the working titles 'Puppet Song' and 'A Hog's Eternity.'
The studio version landed on the band's self-titled 1991 album, their first for Capricorn Records.
This performance opened the second set at the Classic Center in the band's hometown of Athens, Georgia.
The show kicked off a three-night stand celebrating the band's 25th anniversary.
Settle in — this version stretches out to about 13 minutes of dark, funky jamming.
That's Jimmy Herring on lead guitar, holding the chair once occupied by founding guitarist Michael Houser, who died in 2002.
Listen for keyboardist JoJo Hermann steering the jam — his interplay with Herring is the engine of this version.
Frontman John Bell — 'JB' to the faithful — sings lead, as he has since the band's Athens bar-band days.
Drummer Todd Nance is behind the kit here; he remained the band's drummer until the mid-2010s.

title: Pigeons

description: The official live video of the Dead's great farewell song, filmed at Sullivan Stadium in Foxboro, Massachusetts, on July 2, 1989 — Garcia delivering the 'steal your face' chorus to a stadium crowd.

pops.text: Written by Jerry Garcia and Robert Hunter, the Dead's peerless songwriting partnership.
It was first released on the triple live album Europe '72, recorded on the band's spring 1972 European tour.
The song was inspired by a real betrayal: band manager Lenny Hart — drummer Mickey Hart's father — vanished with a large sum of the band's money.
The amount Lenny Hart made off with is commonly put at about $155,000 — a fortune for the band in 1970.
Hear that line, 'steal your face right off your head'? It gave the Dead their 1976 live album title, Steal Your Face.
On Europe '72 the band featured new pianist Keith Godchaux — and Pigpen, on what would be his final tour.
This performance comes from Sullivan Stadium in Foxboro, Massachusetts, July 2, 1989, and was directed by Len Dell'Amico.
That's Brent Mydland on keyboards in this 1989 lineup — just over a year before his death in July 1990.
The full Foxboro concert was screened in 2020 as part of the Dead's Shakedown Stream series, with a Bob Weir pre-show Q&A.
Over the years 'He's Gone' became the band's onstage eulogy — the song they'd play when someone in the Dead family passed away.

title: He's Gone

description: Taylor's self-written, self-directed Opalite video — a film-shot rom-com in which a lonely woman with a pet rock and a lonely man with a pet cactus find each other, cast entirely from one Graham Norton Show sofa.

pops.text: 'Opalite' is track three on The Life of a Showgirl, Taylor Swift's twelfth studio album, released October 3, 2025.
Swift wrote it with Max Martin and Shellback, the Swedish hitmakers behind her biggest pop smashes — all three also produced it.
Opalite is a man-made opal. Swift has linked the title to opal being Travis Kelce's October birthstone — and to the idea of making your own happiness.
It was released as the album's second single in January 2026, following 'The Fate of Ophelia.'
Swift wrote and directed this video herself, shooting on film with cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto.
The entire cast came from one October 2025 episode of The Graham Norton Show, where Swift was a guest promoting the album.
Co-star Domhnall Gleeson joked on that show about wanting to be in a Swift video — she sent him the script within a week.
Swift plays a lonely woman devoted to a pet rock; Gleeson is devoted to a pet cactus. Cillian Murphy voices the fake 'Opalite' infomercial, and Graham Norton himself appears as the salesman.
The video premiered February 6, 2026, exclusively on Spotify Premium and Apple Music, then arrived on YouTube two days later, on Super Bowl Sunday.
In February 2026 the song topped the Billboard Hot 100 — Swift's 14th #1, and her first album with two Hot 100 chart-toppers since 1989 back in 2014.

title: Opalite

description: Bowie's silky funk single from Station to Station — the clip is his famous November 1975 Soul Train performance, which became the song's promo video around the world.

pops.text: 'Golden Years' was the lead single from Station to Station, released November 21, 1975 — while Bowie was still finishing the album.
It was recorded at Cherokee Studios in Los Angeles in September 1975, co-produced by Bowie and Harry Maslin.
It was the first song Bowie recorded for the album — and the first one finished.
Bowie maintained he wrote it for Elvis Presley, who passed on it. His ex-wife Angela claimed it was written for her. Elvis, presumably, never weighed in.
The single climbed to #10 in the US and #8 in the UK.
On November 4, 1975, Bowie mimed this song on Soul Train — only the second white artist ever on the show, after Elton John.
He flubs lines in the performance — Bowie later admitted he hadn't properly learned the song and was embarrassed by the appearance.
That Soul Train clip you're watching became the song's unofficial music video, used for promotion worldwide.
The groove is powered by guitarist Carlos Alomar and the rhythm team of George Murray and Dennis Davis — the unit behind Bowie's late-'70s classics.
A new generation met the song in 2001, when Heath Ledger's dance scene in A Knight's Tale is set to it.

title: Golden Years

description: The official video for the Shabooh Shoobah closer that made INXS internationally famous — a young Michael Hutchence and band in full early-'80s flight.

pops.text: 'Don't Change' was released as a single on October 27, 1982, from INXS's third album, Shabooh Shoobah.
It's the only song on the album credited to all six band members as writers.
Producer Mark Opitz kept the sound lean and urgent — Australian pub-rock energy with new-wave polish.
It has been described as the song that made INXS internationally famous.
In America it only reached #80 on the Hot 100 — but hit #17 on the mainstream rock chart and lived on MTV.
The band formed in Sydney in 1977 as the Farriss Brothers, built around Andrew, Tim and Jon Farriss.
That's Michael Hutchence out front — within a few years he'd be one of rock's defining frontmen.
The song closes Shabooh Shoobah, a final-word anthem: 'Don't change for you, don't change a thing for me.'
This performance video became an early calling card as the band broke outside Australia.
Bruce Springsteen covered 'Don't Change' live in Brisbane in 2014, saluting INXS and Hutchence on their home turf.

title: Don't Change

description: Zeppelin's piano-driven, samba-breaking swerve from In Through the Out Door — no music video or live performance exists, so this is the band's official Atlantic audio upload.

pops.text: The samba idea struck Robert Plant while watching the 1978 World Cup in Argentina on TV, soaking up the stadium rhythms.
It was recorded in late 1978 at Polar Studios in Stockholm — ABBA's studio.
John Bonham's groove is a half-time shuffle modeled on Bernard Purdie's famous 'Purdie shuffle' — drummers still study it note for note.
Midway through, the song breaks down into a full Brazilian samba street-band section, whistles and all.
Jimmy Page's solo runs through an MXR Blue Box octave-fuzz pedal — this solo is still the sound most associated with that stompbox.
John Paul Jones drives the track on piano and co-wrote it with Page and Plant.
Released as a US single on December 7, 1979, it reached #21 on the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1980.
It was the last single Led Zeppelin released before Bonham's death in September 1980 ended the band.
Zeppelin never performed it live — the album arrived after their final UK shows and it missed the 1980 European tour setlist.
Plant finally sang it with a rock band 25 years later, joining Pearl Jam at a 2005 Hurricane Katrina benefit concert in Chicago.

title: Fool in the Rain

description: The official video, filmed on a snowy ski hill at Quebec's Gray Rocks resort — the Police lip-syncing Sting's Trojan-horse sermon about language, dressed for the slopes.

pops.text: Sting wrote this as a comment on how politicians, preachers and pop stars manipulate people with simple language.
Critics dismissed the chorus as baby talk — Sting later called the song 'grossly misunderstood.' That was rather the point.
It's from Zenyatta Mondatta (1980), an album title made of two invented, pseudo-language words — very on-theme.
The single reached #10 on the US Hot 100 and #5 in the UK.
The video was filmed outdoors on a ski hill at the Gray Rocks resort in Quebec's Laurentian Mountains.
The band was in Canada for a Montreal concert that got postponed — with a free day, they shot videos instead.
They filmed two that day: this one, plus an alternate Christmas version of 'Don't Stand So Close to Me.'
The original B-side was drummer Stewart Copeland's spoken-word oddity 'A Sermon.'
Sting re-recorded the song in 1986 as 'De Do Do Do, De Da Da Da '86' — then shelved it until a 1995 singles collection.
The band even cut a Spanish-language version of the song for Spanish-speaking markets.

title: De Do Do Do, De Da Da Da

description: Jeff Stein's surreal Alice in Wonderland video — Petty as the Mad Hatter, Dave Stewart as the hookah-smoking caterpillar, and Alice ending up as cake — for the Southern Accents lead single.

pops.text: Tom Petty co-wrote this with Dave Stewart of Eurythmics — an unlikely Florida-rocker-meets-British-pop pairing.
The title came from a real breakup line: Stewart overheard Stevie Nicks tell Joe Walsh, 'Don't come around here no more.'
Stewart had Nicks in mind for the song — and she still turns up contributing vocals to Petty's version.
That eerie opening hook is Stewart's coral sitar, layered over his synthesizer pulse.
Released in February 1985 as the lead single from Southern Accents, it peaked at #13 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Director Jeff Stein built the video entirely around Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
Petty plays the Mad Hatter; Stewart opens the video as the caterpillar, perched on a mushroom with a hookah, playing sitar.
Actress and singer Louise Foley plays Alice, tumbling into the black-and-white checkerboard tea party.
The video ends with Petty devouring Alice — served as a cake — then burping and wiping his mouth with a napkin.
That abrupt ending chops off the last 29 seconds of guitar solo you hear on the album version.

title: Don't Come Around Here No More

description: No official music video exists — this is the Prince estate's pro-shot live performance from the Carrier Dome in Syracuse, March 30, 1985, on the Purple Rain Tour, with Prince untethered from his guitar and dancing up a storm.

pops.text: 'Darling Nikki' is the fifth track on Purple Rain (1984) — and was never released as a single.
Tipper Gore founded the Parents Music Resource Center after hearing her daughter listening to this song.
'Darling Nikki' topped the PMRC's 'Filthy Fifteen' list of objectionable songs.
The campaign it sparked led directly to the 'Parental Advisory' warning stickers still plastered on albums today.
Stick around for the ending: that eerie choir is backmasked. Played backward it sings, 'Hello, how are you? Fine, fine, 'cause I know that the Lord is coming soon.'
In the Purple Rain film, Prince performs the song at First Avenue specifically to taunt Apollonia.
Session historian Duane Tudahl found the name's origin: Vanity's character in the film was originally to be named Nikki — short for Nicartha Ann.
After Prince became a Jehovah's Witness in 2001, he retired 'Darling Nikki' and his other provocative material from his shows.
This performance was filmed March 30, 1985, at the Carrier Dome in Syracuse, New York, on the Purple Rain Tour.
The Prince estate livestreamed the full Syracuse concert in May 2020 to raise money for COVID-19 relief.

title: Darling Nikki

description: Jonas Åkerlund's official video, filmed at Paris's Charles de Gaulle Airport in August 2000 — Bono running down a runway and the band performing as jets scream overhead.

pops.text: 'Beautiful Day' was the lead single and opening track of All That You Can't Leave Behind (2000), U2's big return-to-basics album.
Bono has said the lyric is about a man who loses everything but still finds joy in what he has left.
It hit #1 in the UK but only #21 in the US — where its real coronation came a few months later.
At the 2001 Grammys it won three awards: Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group.
The video was directed by Jonas Åkerlund, the Swedish director behind some of the era's biggest clips.
It was filmed in August 2000 at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris and premiered the following month.
In the climax, the band performs on the runway itself while passenger jets take off directly overhead — you can hear them scream past.
After 9/11 the song took on a second life as an anthem of resilience in America.
U2 performed it at the Super Bowl XXXVI halftime show in February 2002, with the names of the 9/11 victims scrolling behind the band.
In 2011, astronaut Mark Kelly had the song played in space and dedicated a live performance to his wife, congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords, as she recovered from an assassination attempt.

title: Beautiful Day

description: Anton Corbijn's grainy black-and-white official video for the Bunnymen's 1987 American breakthrough — the band performing in a studio before being transported to a garish Star Trek-style set and hunted by women in space suits. It's the college-radio and MTV 120 Minutes staple from their self-titled fifth album.

pops.text: Released on 20 July 1987, this was the second single from the band's self-titled fifth album, which had arrived two weeks earlier on 6 July.
Ian McCulloch wrote the lyrics; the music is credited to McCulloch, guitarist Will Sergeant and bassist Les Pattinson.
Producer Laurie Latham handled this track, and its B-side was the band-written 'Rollercoaster.'
It charted at #36 in the UK, #24 in Ireland and #43 in New Zealand.
In the US it never charted on the Billboard Hot 100 — yet it became one of the band's most famous songs in America through college radio.
The video was directed by Anton Corbijn and shot in his trademark minimalist, grainy black-and-white style.
Watch the ending: the band is transported from the studio to a garish set straight out of Star Trek, where two women in lurid space suits hunt them.
MTV broadcast the video regularly on its alternative showcase 120 Minutes, helping the song build the band's American audience.

McCulloch initially dismissed it as too commercial — in 1992 he said it 'didn't sound like us' and blamed 'the sound of Radio America' — but by 2005 he conceded the song was strong enough to shine through its 'synthetic twinkles.'
The parent album was the band's last with drummer Pete de Freitas, who died in a motorcycle accident in 1989, aged 27.

title: Lips Like Sugar

description: The official video for the Voices favorite — two minutes and change of pure, bouncing joy from the best-selling duo in music history, later immortalized by a (500) Days of Summer dance number.

pops.text: This comes from Voices (1980), the album where Hall & Oates took over production themselves — and their comeback began.
It was written by Daryl Hall, John Oates and Sara Allen, Hall's longtime girlfriend and writing partner.
Allen also co-wrote the duo's 'Maneater' and 'Private Eyes' — an unsung architect of their sound.
That bouncing riff isn't a guitar — it's a Yamaha CP-30 electric piano.
Released as a single in 1981, it peaked at #5 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Voices also produced the #1 hit 'Kiss on My List' — the duo's first chart-topper.
Hall & Oates are certified by the RIAA as the best-selling music duo of all time.
Hollywood made it a montage staple — it soundtracks Robbie's wedding-planning joy in The Wedding Singer (1998).
Joseph Gordon-Levitt's ecstatic morning-after dance in (500) Days of Summer (2009) introduced it to a whole new generation.
In 2020, four decades after release, the song passed one billion streams worldwide.

title: You Make My Dreams
